findings.title: Cached denial entries block the DB fallback and override newer grants, reintroducing the bug this PR fixes
findings.body: Once a Check is denied, the result is written to permDenialCache with a 30s TTL (shortCacheTTL) and every subsequent Check for the same (user, action, resource, parent) returns deny immediately, without consulting permCache or the database. This defeats the PR's own fix in two ways: (1) if a Check for a newly created dashboard races the permission insert (or hits a lagging read replica, which is the normal deployment for legacysql in cloud), the denial is pinned for 30s and the creator is locked out of the dashboard they just created — the exact symptom the PR claims to fix; (2) when permissions are granted after a denial was recorded (admin grants access, folder moved), the user stays denied for up to 30s even though the database now allows it. Additionally, the denial cache is consulted *before* the positive permCache, so a denial entry written at time T wins over a permCache entry refreshed at T+20 with allowing scopes. There is also no invalidation of denial entries when permissions change. Consider checking the denial cache only after a positive permCache/DB lookup fails, or deleting the denial entry whenever a fresh DB query allows.

findings.title: Denial cache key omits identity type, so anonymous:0 and render:0 share entries
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey is built from namespace, UserUID, action, name and parent — but not the identity type. The subject "anonymous:0" (TypeAnonymous) and "render:0" (TypeRenderService) both parse to UserUID "0", so they produce identical denial keys. Because the denial cache is checked before any identity-type handling, an anonymous user's denial for e.g. dashboards:read on dashboard X (anonymous users can lack read scope on specific dashboards) will cause the render service to be denied rendering of X for up to 30s, even though getRendererPermissions unconditionally grants wildcard read to renderers — and vice versa, a renderer denial of a write action can deny an anonymous user who has that action via a custom Viewer-role permission. Include the identity type in the denial key.

findings.title: Denial cache key concatenates components with '_' without escaping, allowing key collisions
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey joins namespace, userUID, action, name and parent with single underscores and no delimiter escaping. Two different requests can therefore map to the same cache entry, e.g. name="a_b" with parent="c" produces the same key as name="a" with parent="b_c". Today Grafana UIDs are alphanumeric so this is unlikely to trigger, but user/service-account identifiers and future actions are not guaranteed to be underscore-free, and a collision produces a wrong deny verdict for a different resource. Use a separator that cannot appear in the components (or length-prefix/hash the components).

findings.title: Denial cache has unbounded cardinality (one entry per user×action×resource×parent)
findings.body: Unlike permCache, which is bounded per (namespace, user, action), the denial cache creates a distinct entry for every denied (user, action, resource, parent-folder) combination. In the standalone server deployment (RegisterRBACAuthZService) the underlying cache may be a shared external cache (e.g. Redis). A user — or an attacker — enumerating resource names via Check requests will write one denial entry per unknown/unauthorized resource per user, each held for 30s. With batch/Check-heavy clients this can flood the shared cache with garbage entries and cause memory/eviction pressure on the cache cluster. Consider bounding the denial cache (e.g. only caching denials for resources known to exist, using an LRU, or per-user entry limits).

findings.title: No test covering access after a permission is granted post-denial (the issue this PR fixes)
findings.body: TestService_CacheCheck covers allow-from-cache, DB fallback on miss, DB fallback on stale cache, and deny-from-denial-cache, but there is no test for the critical ordering: a denial entry written before a permission was granted (or before the resource existed) versus a later DB/permCache state that allows. Given that the PR's stated purpose is 'creator can't access the dashboard they just created', a test should pin down the expected behavior when a Check for the not-yet-permitted resource precedes the creation/grant — currently that test would fail (deny wins), which suggests the intended semantics are not covered anywhere.
